# Status report: jf2 allocator test in kestrel (2026-11-20)

## Short version

We tested jf2 (our fork of the jemalloc memory allocator) in kestrel (our key-value store) on a read-mostly workload. With jf2, 99th-percentile latency fell from 2140 to 870 microseconds, and throughput stayed within run-to-run variation. Two items remain open: capacity-team approval of 5.7 GB (9.3%) more memory, and the untested write-heavy workload.

## Words used here

- **Build A**: kestrel at commit main@4f1c2aa with jemalloc 5.3.
- **Build B**: the same commit with jf2.
- **ycsb-b, ycsb-a**: workloads B and A of YCSB (Yahoo! Cloud Serving Benchmark). Workload B is read-mostly. Workload A is write-heavy.
- **p50, p99, p99.9**: latency percentiles. For example, 99% of requests finish faster than the p99 value.
- **us**: microseconds.
- **kops/s**: thousand operations per second.
- **RSS**: resident set size, the physical memory that the process holds.
- **decay purge**: the jemalloc step that returns unused memory to the operating system. The function je_arena_decay performs it.
- **latency spike**: a short period of very high latency. A spike window is the time span of one spike.
- **perf**: the Linux sampling profiler.
- **logrotate**: a system job that archives log files. cron (the system scheduler) starts it every night.
- **NUMA pinning**: binding threads and memory to one processor socket. NUMA means non-uniform memory access.
- **feature flag**: a configuration switch that turns a feature on or off.
- **staging**: the pre-production environment.

## Goal

Check whether jf2 fixes the p99 latency spikes in kestrel.

## Setup

- Host: bench-07 (the test host), 2 x 32-core Xeon, 512 GB of memory, Linux kernel 6.8.
- Load average before the runs: 0.4 (nearly idle for 64 cores).
- Workload: ycsb-b with 64 client threads, 10 minutes per run.
- Runs: 5 per build, in alternating order (A, B, A, B, ...).
- The allocator is the only difference between the two builds.

## Results

```
p99 latency, us (1 column = 75 us)
   0        750       1500      2250      3000
   +---------+---------+---------+---------+
A                           |---O-----|        2140 (1890..2610)
B             |O|                              870 (820..940)

p99.9 latency, us (1 column = 375 us)
   0        3750      7500     11250     15000
   +---------+---------+---------+---------+
A                     |------O-----------|     9800 (7200..14100)
B         |O-|                                 3100 (2700..3900)

O = median of 5 runs.  |--| = minimum to maximum run.
```

For both metrics, every B run was faster than every A run. Throughput and p50 latency did not move.

Each value is the median of 5 runs, with the minimum and maximum run in parentheses.

| Metric | Build A (jemalloc 5.3) | Build B (jf2) | Change in median |
|---|---|---|---|
| Throughput, kops/s | 412 (405..418) | 409 (401..415) | −0.7%, ranges overlap |
| p50 latency, us | 118 (116..121) | 119 (117..121) | +0.8%, ranges overlap |
| p99 latency, us | 2140 (1890..2610) | 870 (820..940) | −59% |
| p99.9 latency, us | 9800 (7200..14100) | 3100 (2700..3900) | −68% |
| RSS at end of run, GB | 61.2 (range not recorded) | 66.9 (range not recorded) | +5.7 GB (+9.3%) |

## Findings

1. jf2 lowered p99 and p99.9 latency on ycsb-b.
   - The median p99 fell from 2140 us to 870 us (59% lower) [Ref1].
   - The median p99.9 fell from 9800 us to 3100 us (68% lower) [Ref1].
   - For both metrics, the highest B value is below the lowest A value [Ref1].
2. Throughput and p50 latency did not change measurably.
   - The throughput medians differ by 3 kops/s (0.7%). The A runs alone span 13 kops/s [Ref1].
   - The p50 medians differ by 1 us, and the two ranges overlap [Ref1].
3. Memory use rose with jf2. RSS at the end of the run was 61.2 GB for A and 66.9 GB for B [Ref1]. The difference is 5.7 GB (9.3%).
4. The latency spikes in build A coincide with the decay purge. The perf profile assigned 31% of spike-window samples to je_arena_decay [Ref2].
5. jf2 runs the decay purge in a background thread.
   - Hypothesis: this change is the reason for the lower p99 and p99.9.
   - We have no perf profile of build B, so the link is not confirmed.
   - A perf profile of B's slowest periods would confirm it. It must show no je_arena_decay samples in request-serving threads.

## Data handling

- Run 3 of build B had a 40 s stall at minute 7.
- We traced the stall to logrotate, not to the allocator.
- We reran that run. The table uses the rerun and excludes the stalled run.

## Not tested

- ycsb-a (the write-heavy workload)
- more than 64 client threads
- NUMA pinning

These results apply only to ycsb-b at 64 client threads without NUMA pinning.

## Open decision

The capacity team must decide whether 5.7 GB (9.3%) more RSS is acceptable.

## Next steps

1. Run ycsb-a tomorrow.
2. Ask the capacity team to approve the RSS increase.
3. If they approve, enable jf2 behind a feature flag in staging.

## References

- [Ref1] Results table above: 5 runs per build, ycsb-b, bench-07, 2026-11-20.
- [Ref2] perf profile of build A during its spike windows, same test.

---

Points to check before you send it:

- Your notes give one RSS value per build and no range. The table marks the range as not recorded.
- Your notes hold perf data for build A only. So the report labels the background-purge explanation as a hypothesis.
- I read "if ok" as "if the capacity team approves".
- "Tomorrow" is Saturday 2026-11-21. Change next step 1 if the ycsb-a run is on another day.
